DEFINITION: Credit-claiming is when a senator publicly asserts personal or shared responsibility for a concrete, desirable governmental action, outcome, or benefit—e.g., securing federal funds/grants/projects for the state, obtaining designations/facilities/missions, authoring/sponsoring/shepherding legislation or amendments (introduced, advanced, or enacted), delivering appointments or disaster declarations, or prompting agency action through their intervention.

CLARIFICATION: Include: announcements of federal money or projects flowing to the state/district, even without an explicit "I secured it," because the senator associates themselves with delivering the benefit; explicit statements like "I helped secure," "my amendment," "legislation I authored"; claiming a key role in an outcome (saving a base, expediting a declaration); successful pressure on agencies. Also includes touting one's legislative product (bill introduction/sponsorship centered on the senator's own measure).

NEGATIVE CLARIFICATION: Exclude pure position-taking (statements of opinion, vote explanations, praising/criticizing the President or other parties), ceremonial activities (condolences, remembrances, honoring others, town meeting announcements), advocacy with no achieved outcome and no claimed legislative product (letters, meetings, questions at hearings), welcoming decisions made by others where the senator claims no responsibility, awards given to the senator by outside groups, and partisan credit for collective policies. Incidental biographical credentialing in an otherwise ceremonial release does not qualify.
